Minibatch loss Σ(wℓ)/Σw is a ratio estimator. With parameter-independent weights, SGD optimizes E_batch[Σ(wℓ)/Σw], generally different from E[Σ(wℓ)]/E[Σw]. Self-normalized importance sampling has finite-sample bias; consistency concerns increasing batch size, not additional training steps at fixed batch size. Recency weights alone are not importance corrections unless they encode a target-to-sampling probability ratio. [BR-SNIS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.06364) discusses this normalization bias.

Applied to random crops: let I_ut indicate that crop C includes user u’s target t, and π_ut=P(I_ut=1). With fixed per-user denominator Z_u, the expected contribution is Σ_t π_ut w_ut E[ℓ_ut(C) | I_ut=1]/Z_u. Choosing Z_u=Σ_t π_ut w_ut gives each sampled user unit total coefficient mass while retaining crop-induced target exposure. Choosing Z_u=Σ_t w_ut instead gives users different total mass according to exposure. Crop-dependent normalization produces coefficients E[I_ut w_ut/Σ_s I_us w_us], generally unequal to π_ut w_ut/Σ_s π_us w_us. Per-crop normalization equalizes crop mass; batch-global normalization lets crops/users with greater weight sums contribute more. These are mathematical deductions from the sampling design.

For a desired full-history recency objective, use inverse-inclusion contributions I_ut w_ut/π_ut with fixed Z_u=Σ_t w_ut; positive inclusion probabilities are required. This follows the [Horvitz–Thompson estimator](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0378375819301211). Compute π_ut from the actual endpoint/length sampler: for uniformly sampled length-L contiguous windows over n eligible targets, π_ut equals the number of valid windows containing t divided by n−L+1. Cropping also changes context, so inclusion correction recovers a crop-context-averaged objective, not automatically full-context training.
